frames.narration: A page needs 12 files. With HTTP/1.1 the browser opens about six connections, each with its own handshake, and each connection handles one request at a time.

messages.label: 6 connections, 2 files each, one after another

frames.narration: Every file has to wait for the one before it on its connection. The page is slow because of waiting, not because of the size of the files.
HTTP/2 uses a single connection and a single handshake. All 12 requests are sent at once as interleaved streams, and the server answers them in parallel.
But all the streams share one TCP connection. A single lost packet stops TCP from delivering anything after it, so every stream stalls until the retransmission arrives.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which tracks loss per stream. The same lost packet now delays only the one stream it belonged to. The other 11 keep flowing.
QUIC also sets up transport and encryption in a single round trip, and in zero round trips when the browser has connected before. A phone moving from Wi-Fi to mobile data keeps the same connection.
